We see from the largest value in the table (indicated in bold) that ϵ = 2.337. While this simple example only included one protected dimension (Group 1 vs Group 2), differential fairness is designed to be applied to scenarios where there are multiple protected dimensions to consider at once (e.g., gender, race, and nationality).

Due to its relationship with differential privacy, differential fairness provides a privacy guarantee—the class label assigned by the model will not reveal much information about the protected attributes if the definition holds (i.e., ϵ is small). More concretely, consider a scenario where the users’ data is held on a private server and a bank, assumed untrustworthy, is told only the output of a classifier that predicts whether an individual will repay a loan. The privacy guarantee ensures that, for example, if the individual is predicted to repay the loan the bank cannot conclude that the user is probably White and male.

Differential fairness has a generalization guarantee but it is weaker than the one for subgroup fairness; the fairness parameter ϵ estimated from the training data will generalize to the overall population as long as there is enough data for each intersectional subgroup. The differing goals of subgroup fairness and differential fairness led to the differing treatment of small subgroups in the two metrics. Subgroup fairness aims to prevent any attempt to gerrymander the fairness behavior of the algorithm, so it assumes that there are many dimensions and prioritizes generalization over ensuring that minority subgroups are protected. Differential fairness aims to ensure an intersectional conception of fairness, so it prioritizes minority subgroups over generalization. The number of protected dimensions, and hence the number of subgroups, need not be so large since the goal is to have a more nuanced understanding of fairness beyond considering top-level protected groups separately (e.g., women, Black people). Intersectionality was originally inspired by harms that occur at the intersection of two protected attributes (gender, race). From an intersectional perspective, even just the consideration of these two dimensions is already an improvement over the status quo.

Alternatively, the multicalibration fairness metric ensures that the prediction probabilities are calibrated for all the protected subgroups of interest. We discussed calibration earlier as a limitation of the equalized odds fairness definition; multicalibration aims to address this particular issue for overlapping subgroups.

A different approach to solving the fairness gerrymandering issue is to remove the notion of groups from the fairness definition entirely and focus on individuals directly. Individual fairness, proposed by Cynthia Dwork and colleagues, embodies the ideal that similar individuals should be treated similarly by the algorithm by having similar class probabilities. Encoding this mathematically results in the following definition. Suppose we have a distance measure d(x,y) between pairs of data points x, y (e.g., Euclidean distance) and a distance measure between pairs of probability distributions over class labels D(μx,μy), for example, Jensen-Shannon divergence. We assume that our classifier of interest M(x) is a probabilistic classifier such as logistic regression, which randomly assigns a class label to each instance x according to the class probabilities it outputs. The individual fairness criterion holds if similar data points have similar outcome probabilities, that is,

D(M(x),M(y)) ≤ d(x,y). (7.18)

(7.18)

This constraint can be made into a fairness penalty by measuring the extent to which the inequality is violated, instead of rigidly enforcing the equality. A key challenge in implementing individual fairness in practice is that we need to define the distance between individuals in a way that is fair, which is far from straightforward. Perhaps a subset of the features that are deemed to be “fair” could be used for this measurement. The chosen features would have to accurately represent the “deservingness” of the individuals (since otherwise two “similar” individuals should not necessarily get similar class probabilities) while not encoding demographic proxies.

Incompatibility Between Fairness Definitions

We have considered several fairness definitions, each of which is frequently a desirable property for the behavior of an AI system. It would be wonderful if we could design our AI system to satisfy all of these definitions simultaneously, while also accurately predicting the class labels and producing calibrated probability estimates. Unfortunately, as you might expect, this is not always possible. There are mathematical theorems proving that many of these fairness definitions are in some cases incompatible with each other and/or with predictive accuracy or calibration. Such incompatibilities often arise when the protected demographics have different base rates (probabilities of the class labels) and/or when perfect prediction (the model assigning each data point to its correct class with class probabilities that are certain) is not possible. From a practical perspective, the upshot is that when we design a fair machine learning system, we must work with stakeholders to decide on the appropriate fairness metric(s) and the appropriate balance with predictive performance.

Fair Representation Learning

Instead of defining and measuring fairness by quantifying it with some function, another approach is to preprocess the data by replacing all of the features with embeddings in which all associations and correlations with the protected attributes are excised while otherwise retaining as much information in the embeddings as possible. In other words, we perform representation learning (i.e., learning embedding representations of the data) but do so in a way that aims to ensure fairness for any downstream analysis. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this methodology is called fair representation learning. We will discuss representation learning in Chapter 10, “Deep learning: fundamentals.”

This is typically achieved based on adversarial learning methods such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) or variational autoencoders (VAEs), which we will cover in Chapter 11, “Advanced deep learning methods.” Without getting too far ahead of ourselves, suppose we are training a deep neural network classifier to predict class labels y based on input data x. An individual with data xi has sensitive or protected demographic attributes si. We further assume that as part of the classification process, the deep neural network learns embedding representations zi of the data points, which will be used to predict yi. Now, for the purpose of making the embeddings fair, we introduce another classifier, an “adversary,” that tries to predict the protected attributes si based on zi.

If the adversary is well trained then it would find and exploit any relationship between the zi’s and the si’s. On the other hand, if the deep neural network classifier successfully learns zi’s that have no associations with the protected attributes si, then the adversary will be unable to predict the si’s. We can train the deep neural network classifier to simultaneously predict the class labels yi and to “fool” the adversary by learning zi’s that the adversary performs poorly on while jointly training the adversary. This is a typical GAN-based approach to fair representation learning. The VAE-style approach is similar, but instead of trying to fool an adversary the deep learning classifier is encouraged, via architecture choices and penalty functions, to learn zi’s that are statistically independent from the si’s. This strategy is closely related to disentangled representation learning, in which the features that are learned are independent from each other and hence more interpretable as the distinct meaningful factors that underly a dataset, for example, the lighting, pose, and orientation of an image.

Causal Fairness

In the real world, unfair outcomes happen for a reason. There are processes that systematically advantage some and disadvantage others, such as the impact of sexism on hiring outcomes. In the parlance of intersectionality theory, these processes are called systems of oppression. Ideally, to make an AI system fair, we ought to understand and model these systems and account for them when determining and correcting unfairness. This is difficult work, as these processes work in subtle and pernicious ways that are not always recorded digitally, and so it may be difficult to construct a model of the data and its unfairness patterns that is accurate and uncontroversial to stakeholders, who likely all have different value systems and assumptions about the world. This difficulty motivates all the other, typically easier, methodologies that we have considered thus far.

If we do decide to undertake the task of modeling all the reasons for unfairness in data and algorithms, causal modeling is a key tool as it allows us to understand and represent the causal relationship between the relevant variables. Causality hinges on the concept of an intervention to a system—if we were to give a drug to a patient would they be more likely to recover from their disease? In practice, we don’t always have the ability to perform such interventions; rather, the data we receive is observational, collected through the natural course of events without intervening. Causal inference is the task of trying to figure out the causal phenomena that would have occurred if we could have performed the appropriate interventions, based only on the observational data that we have. An even more difficult task, causal discovery, aims to construct a full causal model of the cause-and-effect relationships between all relevant variables in a problem domain.

Supposing that we can successfully model the causal structure of the problem domain, causal fairness methodologies intervene on the AI algorithm to achieve causal properties that are deemed fair. One such property, called counterfactual fairness, supposes that we could intervene on an individual’s protected attributes (e.g., their gender or race). In doing so we would be in another world where things are different from the actual world; this is called a counterfactual world. With a causal model in hand we could estimate how things would be different in the counterfactual world. A decision for an individual is said to be counterfactually fair if, in a counterfactual world where we intervened to change the individual’s protected attributes, the probabilities of the outcomes (e.g., class labels) would not be altered. If you were a man instead of a woman (or vice-versa) would the bank have offered you a loan? Or, if you were White instead of Asian (or vice-versa) would the company have offered you a job?

Practical Guidelines for Fair Machine Learning

We’ve seen quite a few fairness definitions and methodologies but you might still be feeling quite unsure about how to design a fair machine learning system in practice. This is natural, as fairness is a complex, multistakeholder issue. Indeed, feeling uncertain about this is a good thing. As a technologist or engineer, it’s important to practice humility regarding your understanding of the nontechnical aspects of the sociotechnical context that an AI system lives in and the limitations of purely technological solutions to simply “solve” AI fairness. The last thing you should ever do is to show up as some kind of technology wizard and hand down a technological fairness intervention, as if from on-high, to “fix” an AI system without talking to anyone who is impacted by the system or examining the likely (and actual) impacts of your intervention. Well, okay, this is probably slightly better than not considering fairness and bias issues at all, but only marginally so. This is a good time to re-emphasize that it is vital to include stakeholders in the design of a fair and responsible AI/ML (machine learning) system, as we have discussed. In addition, we will go over a few things to consider in the practical design of fair machine learning systems.

Understanding Fairness and Bias in Your Problem Domain

We have seen that many options for mathematical fairness definitions exist. These alternative fairness definitions:

  • • May encode differing goals about fairness;
  • • May make differing assumptions about the real world and ideal world;
  • • May be desirable to different stakeholders, who may have conflicting goals; and
  • • May or may not correct the underlying fairness problems (or even make them worse).

It’s important to remember that no single fairness definition is applicable in all cases! Before attempting a fairness intervention, we first need to perform a careful reflection on the fairness and bias issues in the problem domain at hand. What are the likely sources of bias in the data, and hence in the algorithm? Is there a history of prejudice or unfair practices that needs to be accounted for? We need to stop and think about:

  • • Who is being harmed:
    • • By larger societal processes that impact the data?
    • • By data quality and selection issues?
    • • By the system itself?
  • • Why are they harmed?

Some considerations in defining fairness include:

  • • Are we addressing harms of representation, in which a model perpetuates harmful stereotypes that represent a protected group in a hurtful way? Or are we addressing harms of outcome, in which the predictions of the model are used for decision making, whose outcomes cause tangible or economic harm? As an example, the sentiment classifier that assigns negative sentiment to stereotypically Black names, which we discussed, creates a harm of representation because it perpetuates hurtful, racist opinions in the way that it represents people. On the other hand, if we used that same sentiment classifier to analyze resumes and it led to fewer Black people being offered a job interview, this would be a harm of outcome.
  • • In the present context, should fairness correspond to equality between protected groups, or are there legitimate reasons why equality is not the ideal solution, such as confounding factors or differing levels of qualification? One example of this situation arose in a study of admissions to the University of California Berkeley in the 1970s. The study found that while women were admitted to the University at a rate less than for men, this was explained by the fact that women tended to apply to departments that were more selective compared to men. When analyzing the results on a per-department basis, women were generally admitted at a higher rate than men. This counter-intuitive and impossible-sounding scenario is in fact possible due to a phenomenon known as Simpson’s paradox. The study concluded that there was no gender bias in the admissions process. Psychological research has concluded that when “fairness” (in a meritocratic sense) is in conflict with equality, humans tend to prioritize fairness over equality. If (meritocratic) fairness conflicts with equality, we must reckon with how to balance these competing goals.
  • • Are there underlying differences between protected groups, and should we accept the consequences of those differences in the data or correct for those differences? In research on discriminatory decision making in criminal justice contexts such as risk scores for recidivism, for example, some researchers have argued that since different demographic groups have different distributions over features, they would be expected to have different distributions over idealized risk scores (e.g., the probability of committing a crime). This phenomenon is termed infra-marginality. Proponents of this theory argue that because of the different distributions of risk between demographic groups, which are assumed to be legitimate, meritocratic, and well estimated, differences in outcome probabilities or error rates between demographic groups may not correspond to unfair discrimination. On the other hand, if the differences in risk are due to unfair reasons, we should not necessarily take the implications of those differences at face value.
  • • Should we aim to correct biases in society, beyond biases in data? In other words, should our intervention aim to perform fair affirmative action?

Does Your Problem Definition Contain Bias?

When solving a real-world problem through data mining, we must convert the problem into a question that data mining can solve, which is typically the prediction of a target variable via classification or regression models. The process of defining the data mining problem is a stage in which we might inadvertently introduce bias, that is, by making a decision that systematically disadvantages or advantages a protected demographic group. In many cases the class variable is selected because it is a conveniently measurable proxy for the thing we actually care about. For instance, in credit scoring the measurable class variable “this person repaid a loan” is used as a proxy for something more elusive, “this person should be given a loan.” It is important to remember that this is a proxy that was chosen for convenience and should not be viewed as the absolute, objective, and definitive final word on creditworthiness. More generally, we must be careful that the choice of class variable is not harmful. In hiring, the probability of employee retention might be used as a proxy for whether to interview or hire a candidate. If employee retention is higher for some demographics than others (e.g., women leaving the technology sector more frequently than men due to facing workplace discrimination), using employee retention as the prediction target would result in systematically offering fewer positions to women.

The Framing Trap

Once we have converted our real-world problem to a data mining problem, it is easy to forget that the system we build to solve the data mining problem exists in a bigger real-world context. Failing to consider this broader sociotechnical context, of which the machine learning system is but one component, is called the framing trap. If we do not consider how the outputs of our machine learning model are used in real-world decision making, and what the flow-on effects of those decisions are, we will not be able to make the broader sociotechnical system completely fair in an end-to-end sense. For example, in bail and sentencing decisions recidivism risk scores that are made by an AI system are generally given to a judge as mere recommendations, and the judge makes the final decision. The judge may be subject to automation bias in which they accept the algorithm’s recommendations without appropriate critique, they may ignore the algorithm’s recommendations entirely, or they may deviate from the recommendations in systematically biased ways. A fairness intervention on the AI system may thus not have the desired effect, such as provoking a response by the judge to overcompensate for the AI fairness intervention with even more biased behavior.

Navigating Fairness Trade-Offs

Since fairness penalties compete with predictive accuracy in a fair machine learning algorithm’s objective function (Equation 7.7), there is usually a trade-off between fairness and accuracy, as we illustrate in Fig. 7.8. This is particularly the case when parity-based fairness metrics are used, since if there is disparity between demographic groups in the data the enforcing parity would be at odds with making accurate predictions. In this case it would be wise to engage impacted stakeholders along with business stakeholders to negotiate a compromise solution. Fairness hyperparameters such as λ in Equation 7.7, and potentially other model hyperparameters, can be tuned to select the appropriate trade-off.

When tuning fairness hyperparameters, it is useful to first calculate the accuracy and/or the fairness measurement of the original (“typical”) machine learning model without a fairness intervention. With that information at hand, we can then threshold one of these quantities to a minimum acceptable value while optimizing the other via a grid search (or a more sophisticated hyperparameter tuning strategy such as Bayesian optimization). We can threshold the minimum accuracy (or other performance measure) to be at least, say, 95% of the accuracy of typical machine learning model while making the fairness metric as good as possible while satisfying that constraint. Alternatively, we can threshold the fairness metric (e.g., satisfying the 80% rule) while optimizing accuracy.

The prevailing “folk wisdom” is that fairness must always come at a cost of some degree of predictive performance based on the intuition in Fig. 7.8. However, this is not the case. Often it is possible to obtain “fairness for free,” where a fairness metric is improved at no cost to predictive performance. Reasons for the fairness for free phenomenon include:

  • • Fairness penalties can act as a regularizer. They have the potential to reduce overfitting, hence improving generalization performance on unseen data.
  • • Multiple classifiers can potentially obtain same or similar numbers of errors. For example, many deep learning models with completely different weights may have essentially the same predictive performance. This is called the Rashomon effect. Some of those equally accurate classifiers may be fairer than others. We can therefore potentially choose between these classifiers to “gerrymander” the errors so that the system is fairer (see Fig. 7.9).

We show an example of fairness for free via the Rashomon effect in. The classifiers with the solid and dashed hyperplanes both make two errors (indicated with solid and dashed circles, respectively). However, the solid-line classifier makes two errors on instances from the same demographic group (indicated via shading) while the dashed-line classifier makes errors on instances from different demographic groups. While this example may seem contrived, practical experience with training deep neural networks—which generally converge to any number of local optima or saddle points of a highly nonconvex objective function but obtain similar performance across runs—suggests that for these models there are many different solutions with similar predictive performance. Of these similar quality solutions, we can and should aim to pick the fairest option.

In practice, it is frequently possible to obtain fairness for free via the following strategy:

  1. 1. Perform a grid search on the hyperparameters of the “typical” machine learning model (without a fairness intervention) and record the predictive accuracy P of the best model on the validation set.
  2. 2. Perform a grid search on the fair machine learning model over all the hyperparameters including both the fairness trade-off hyperparameter λ as well as other model hyperparameters.
  3. 3. Based on the grid search, select the model with the best fairness parameter out of those that have predictive accuracy equal to or better than P.

Important Caveats to Fair AI/Data Mining

When employing fairness interventions it is essential to remember the limitations of the fair AI paradigm. A mathematical definition cannot, by itself, solve the sociotechnical problem of “fairness,” which has nontechnical dimensions and exceeds the narrowly defined AI/data mining system. Humans, including impacted stakeholders and experts from other fields such as law, the humanities, sociology, philosophy, psychology, and so on, must be part of the solution. The sociotechnical context in which an AI system is embedded must always be accounted for. The fair AI paradigm arguably oversimplifies complex sociotechnical problems to straightforward technical ones.

Even worse, fair AI technologies could potentially legitimize problematic systems by providing a veneer of ethical respectability to them. There are some systems that should never be deployed, no matter how much we intervene to make them fair. Affect-recognition systems, for example, are AI-based computer vision systems that analyze video, image, or audio data to detect emotions such as fear or anger. These systems have been deployed for applications in hiring, law enforcement, casinos, restaurants, hospitals, prisons, and beyond. As you might expect by now, many of these systems are racially biased. Some scholars have argued that the ethical issues with these systems run deeper and the surveillance they facilitate is harmful in and of itself. It has also been argued that these systems lack scientific validity, with the facial movement data they rely on being insufficient to determine emotion to the degree of accuracy required for their intended applications. In one view, correcting racial bias issues in affect-recognition systems would not be enough to make the systems acceptable for deployment in many of their intended use-cases.

Human-centered computing researcher Os Keyes and colleagues penned a scathing satire of the fair AI paradigm that serves to illustrate some of its limitations. They imagine an AI system that selects older adults with low social credit as candidates for being mulched into a high-nutrient slurry. If you have ever seen the film Soylent Green, which imagines a future in which humans are turned into food, you will understand the concept. In this scenario, an AI fairness analysis finds that White cisgender men are much more likely to be selected for mulching compared to other demographics. They perform an AI fairness intervention to correct this “bias” by increasing the mulching probability for all other demographics such as transgender women, Asian Americans, and so on, to match the high mulching probability of White cisgender men. They ensure that the system is adequately transparent in its decision making by publicly releasing the set of variables that were used to select “mulches”—phone and text message metadata, the number of Facebook friends, the number of birthday cards received, and so on. The system is made accountable, as the prospective mulchees can speak to a phone operator about factors of social credit the system may have overlooked that could be included in the next version of the system. The authors conclude that their system is fair, accountable, and transparent while working to solve the problem of food security, and so it must therefore be beyond all possible ethical reproach!

7.3 AI Safety

As AI becomes more sophisticated and inscrutable, there are rising concerns that AI and machine learning technologies can behave in dangerous and unintended ways. These issues arise in large part because it is difficult to fully specify and control the behavior of a system that is learned rather than programmed to ensure that it behaves as we want it to. This issue is called the AI alignment problem.

The AI Alignment Problem

I really hate this damn machine,

I wish that they would sell it.

It never does quite what I want,

But only what I tell it.

—Anonymous

Some of you may have heard this quote, with unknown attribution, in one of your first programming classes. Any programmer quickly learns that it is difficult to perfectly tell a computer exactly what you want it to do, and a slight misstep in specifying its instructions could lead to disastrous results.

A similar issue can occur when designing an AI or machine learning system. The AI alignment problem, sometimes called the value alignment problem, is the problem that the objective function that a human specifies for an AI may not perfectly correspond to their intended behavior and goals for the system, and it could admit unintended consequences. There is a fairly direct analogy to stories of a genie or other supernatural entity that grants wishes, but the stated wish has a loophole that causes it to backfire and come true with unforeseen negative results. The story of King Midas, who was granted his wish that everything he touches turns to gold, is a canonical example.

AI alignment problems can happen due to unintended side effects. The AI fairness and bias issues that we discussed fall into this category; a machine learning system may accurately predict the target class label while also exhibiting harmful behavior such as unfair discriminatory patterns in its predictions. This is an alignment issue because a machine learning objective function that only rewards accurate predictions fails to rule out biased behavior.

As previously discussed in this chapter, class labels are often chosen as convenient proxies for ground truth, such as repaying a loan as a proxy for a more holistic notion of creditworthiness, and these choices can impair alignment in a manner that introduces discriminatory bias. When an AI system has a real-world physical presence, direct physical harm becomes a possibility, that is, a self-driving car that runs over pedestrians to reach its destination or a robot vacuum cleaner that knocks over tables while cleaning.

Misaligned AI issues can also occur from specification gaming, also known as reward hacking, in which the AI system achieves its goal via a novel and unforeseen strategy that was not intended by the system’s designer. Humans do this, too. If a restaurant manager punishes her staff whenever they are seen to not be actively working, employees are incentivized to do their assigned tasks as slowly as possible. The employee may achieve this by cleaning surfaces in the least efficient order, with the gunk in the microwave falling onto the microwave stand and further down to the counter below so that both surfaces must be cleaned again, creating unnecessary work that allows the worker to appear busy when they are not.

Researcher Victoria Krakovna maintains a list of examples of specification gaming on her blog if you would like to see many instances of the phenomenon. In one case, reported by Twitter user Custard Smingleigh, a Roomba robot vacuum cleaner was trained to drive using a neural network via reinforcement learning with rewards for speed and for not setting off its bumper sensors that indicate a collision. Since there were no sensors on the back, the AI learned to travel at high speed in reverse, thus avoiding penalties for any collisions.

This example shows how it can be difficult for humans to perfectly specify the desired behavior of an AI system, resorting instead to simpler proxy goals that may or may not lead to the intended results. One possible solution to this challenge is to learn the reward function, from human feedback or imitation learning methodologies such as inverse reinforcement learning, but this can create its own specification gaming issues. For example, researchers from OpenAI created a reinforcement learning algorithm that learns preferred behaviors from human feedback and used it to train a robot hand to grasp a ball. However, the AI instead learned to fool human annotators by simply placing the hand between the ball and the observer, appearing to grasp it but not actually doing so.

Of course, unanticipated solutions can be desirable and are a sign that the learning algorithm is powerful enough to find solutions that go beyond what the human designers could dream up. When Google Deepmind’s AlphaZero system was trained to play chess it produced novel and effective game-playing strategies that human players did not know about. Whether a novel solution is desirable, or if it constitutes unwanted specification gaming, can be a complicated question. One of the authors was once told of a case where an airport hired academic consultants to help them reduce the time that passengers were waiting to claim their baggage. The problem was formalized as a mathematical optimization problem with the objective of minimizing the passengers’ wait time. The optimization algorithm produced a solution in which the passengers had to walk all the way across the airport to retrieve their baggage, thereby waiting next to the carousel for a shorter time. This solution seems perverse as it did not actually get the baggage back to the passengers any faster. However, the airport implemented it and the complaints by the passengers went away!

While it is difficult enough to specify the objective or reward function of an AI system well enough that the solution to the optimization problem is sure to be what we want (outer alignment), further AI alignment problems can arise when the system learns that it must achieve intermediate goals to achieve its objectives (inner alignment). A robot vacuum cleaner that aims to clean an entire house must learn to identify doorways and navigate between the rooms of the house, for instance. We typically train machine learning algorithms by optimizing some objective function but the models that are learned could themselves be optimizers (e.g., learning to efficiently navigate the house). Such a model is called a mesa-optimizer. Alignment problems can occur if the learned intermediate goals that a mesa-optimizer aims to achieve are the result of overfitting, called goal mis-generalization. For example, if an intelligent agent seeks a coin that is always in the same location in its training data but that coin is in a different location at test time, it may blindly navigate to the original location and might not even recognize the coin in its new location.

One intermediate emergent goal that arises naturally and can help an AI system achieve many goals is to obtain power over its environment by increasing its resources or its ability to prevent any other agent or human from impeding it. Such power-seeking behavior has clear and obvious risks. The robot vacuum cleaner might learn how to lock all humans in the house in a closet so that they cannot create a mess, for example. It could learn how to evade being switched off (which would prevent it from completing its cleaning), potentially by harming or deceiving humans.

The potential tendency of many different AI systems to seek power is an example of instrumental convergence. An instrumental goal is one that is a means to an end. Instrumental convergence occurs when multiple intelligent agents (AI or human) seek the same useful subgoal (e.g., obtaining power) to achieve each of their varied goals. This could potentially lead to harmful results. In the famous paperclip maximizer thought experiment by philosopher Nick Bostrom, for example, we suppose that an AI is tasked with producing as many paperclips as possible. The AI quickly determines that humans might switch it off, thus preventing it from creating paperclips, and the humans also contain atoms that are useful for creating paperclips. Its goal of maximizing the number of paperclips is in direct conflict with a world in which there are many living humans so it achieves its intermediate goal with catastrophic results.

Artificial Superintelligence and the Threat of Rogue AI

Could an AI really exterminate all human life or enslave us all? An AI like the paperclip maximizer might not need to be more intelligent than humans, and certainly wouldn’t need to be considered “conscious,” to accomplish this if it could obtain sufficient resources. However, if humans could outsmart it, it might not succeed. An artificial superintelligence (ASI) is a hypothetical AI that is more intelligent than humans. This should not be confused with a related concept—artificial general intelligence (AGI), a hypothetical AI that is general enough to perform well over many tasks and problem domains, while not necessarily being more “intelligent” than humans. Some authors have argued that large language models (LLMs), which can solve tasks ranging from mathematics, to medicine, to law, and beyond, are already at the beginning stages of AGI.

If we subscribe to the functionalist theory of mind, which states that minds and mental states depend on the functional roles of the system that they are a part of, then the human brain is just one possible piece of hardware that could produce a mind, and we could presumably implement a mind using different hardware such as a digital computer. This would imply that, in principle, ASI is possible and therefore might one day be a threat to human existence and/or autonomy. The view that AI is a near-term threat to human existence is a controversial position but it has its proponents, including prominent technologists such as entrepreneur Elon Musk and the late theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking. One of the most credible voices to take this position is deep learning pioneer Geoff Hinton, who resigned (some might say retired) at age 75 from Google in 2023 to have the freedom to warn about these kinds of risks. Hinton took this view after being alarmed by the recent rapid progress of LLMs in their ability to acquire general knowledge and perform reasoning. A persistent theory, notably advocated by professor and science fiction author Vernor Vinge and futurist Ray Kurzweil, is that a phenomenon known as the singularity will occur, referring to a hypothetical scenario in which technological progress will enable its own runaway acceleration, leading to consequences that are so far beyond our current understanding that they are difficult to comprehend or foresee.

On the other hand, all technological trends to date have reached a point of diminishing returns, and LLMs are unlikely to be an exception to this rule. If, as most computer scientists believe, P ≠ NP, then many AI problems are fundamentally difficult to solve and thus there are limits to what an AI might accomplish, no matter how well designed. Many AI researchers have learned from bitter experience—in struggling to achieve a few percentage points of improvement on benchmark tasks to get our work published—that progress in the field is really difficult and comes with much human blood, sweat, and tears. While the rapid advances in LLM technology have been unexpected and astounding, this situation has not fundamentally changed.

Moreover, even if ASI could be developed, an overemphasis on the importance of intelligence may be naïve. Wired Magazine founding editor Kevin Kelly calls this the “thinkism fallacy.” No matter how smart an AI is, for it to find a cure for cancer it would not only need to come up with a good idea for a cure but also perform medical trials to test its hypothesis and likely adjust its approach many times based on the data from the trials before succeeding. In 2015, renowned AI expert Andrew Ng said, “The reason I say that I don’t worry about AI turning evil is the same reason I don’t worry about overpopulation on Mars.” While much has changed since then, it is still true that there are many immediate and urgent concerns around AI that need to be addressed right now. While some concern for the more distant future may be warranted, we should not let that lead us to neglect the present. Prominent AI researcher Meredith Whittaker, who was forced out of Google for organizing against the company’s drone computer vision contracts with the US military (although Google disputes this account of events), has argued that “alarmist” views such as those expressed by Hinton have a very real cost in terms of deprioritizing AI fairness and equity issues. She expressed dismay that Hinton and others at Google warned against hypothetical future risks from AI but did not support efforts to curtain the harms due to AI that are already happening, which fall disproportionately on women, people of color, and especially women of color. We discussed AI bias and fairness issues earlier in this chapter, and in Sections 15.10 and 15.11 we’ll expand our discussion to other such concerns at the intersection of AI and our society.

7.4 Further Reading and Bibliographic Notes

Useful discussions on the definition of privacy in the big data era are given by Richards and King (2014), and Solove (2010). Sweeney (2000) provided a compelling census-data example of the problem linkage attacks pose to anonymized data. The k-anonymity technique is also due to Sweeney (2002). Machanavajjhala et al. (2006) illustrated several attacks that can defeat k-anonymity. Differential privacy is due to Dwork (2006), with a more comprehensive treatment given in Dwork and Roth (2014). Abadi et al. (2016) developed a practical technique for differentially private deep learning, including the moments accountant technique for efficiently keeping track of how sequential differentially privacy operations use up a privacy budget. Federated learning was proposed by Konečný et al. (2015).

Much of what we know about AI fairness and bias issues from real systems was revealed by journalists. Fairness issues in criminal justice risk assessments were exposed by investigative journalists Angwin et al. (2016), who used a freedom of information request to obtain data on the COMPAS system. Dastin (2018) described the case of Amazon’s internal recruiting tool that was biased against women. Researchers have also weighed in and Bulamwini and Gebru (2018) analyzed bias at the intersection of gender and skin tone in facial recognition systems, further validated in follow-up work from NIST by Grother et al. (2019). Many other detailed examples of problems with AI-based decisions were given by O’Neill (2017). The ACM’s statement on principles for responsible algorithmic systems, including AI-based systems, was published by ACM Technology Policy Office (2022). In a blog post, Speer (2017) provided a compelling example of how bias issues can arise unintentionally in natural language processing (NLP) systems. Common sources of AI bias are illustrated in depth by Barocas and Selbst (2016). Noble (2018) gives a detailed account of representation issues in the output of algorithms, focusing on Google search.

The main fair AI paradigm, in which fairness metrics are enforced in a learning algorithm, is due to Dwork et al. (2012). The authors proposed the individual fairness metric and considered and critiqued differential parity fairness. The 80% rule, a legal criterion for discrimination with a parity flavor and that can be used for fair AI, was codified by the US Equal Employment Opportunities Commission in C.F.R. 29.1607 (EEOC, 1978), and corresponding machine learning algorithms were developed by Zafar et al. (2017). The equalized odds and equality of opportunity fairness definitions, which aim to address some of the issues with parity-based fairness, were proposed by Hardt et al. (2016). While authors including Hardt et al. and Simoiu et al. (2017) criticized parity-based fairness metrics, Foulds and Pan (2020) discussed both sides of the argument and defended the concept of parity-based fairness. Pleiss et al. (2017) showed a key limitation of equalized odds fairness, namely that it is incompatible with calibrated probability estimates. The incompatibility and resulting trade-offs between fairness definitions were earlier analyzed by Kleinberg et al. (2016). Fair representation learning was proposed by Zemel et al. (2013). A canonical example of the use of adversarial learning for fair representations was developed by Beutel et al. (2017). A blog post by Tonk (2018), which applies the methods of Louppe et al. (2017) to fairness, is also recommended reading on this topic. Kusner et al. (2017) developed the first, and most prominent, causal fairness method, counterfactual fairness.

The consideration of fairness at the intersection of protected groups can be motivated by intersectionality, a framework for analyzing systemic patterns of injustices and how they interact with overlapping protected demographic dimensions, due to Crenshaw (1989). Kearns et al. (2018) proposed subgroup fairness, which aims to ensure fairness at the intersection of multiple protected groups, and was not informed by intersectionality theory but rather aims to prevent subset targeting, a.k.a. fairness gerrymandering. Foulds et al. (2020); Islam et al. (2023) critiqued subgroup fairness from the perspective of intersectionality and proposed the first definition that was explicitly motivated by intersectionality. Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018) proposed multicalibration, another fairness definition for overlapping protected groups that focuses on calibrated probability estimates.

An important strand of work critiques the limitations of the AI fairness paradigm, and this work is often insightful for how one ought to use (or not use) AI fairness interventions in practice. Blogdett et al. (2020) provided a critical review of fair NLP research, which went beyond summarizing the papers to pointing to the serious deficiencies in that subfield, and in fair ML more generally in terms of addressing the broader context of who has been harmed by a system and what a fair system should actually do. Selbst et al. (2019) shone a spotlight on the importance of accounting for the sociotechnical context that an AI system is embedded in and the pitfalls that can arise because of it, such as the framing trap. Keyes et al. (2019) critiqued the shortcomings of the dominant fairness, accountability, and transparency (FAT) framework with a scathing satirical example. Islam et al. (2021) showed that despite the conventional wisdom in the field, it is frequently possible, and indeed easy, to obtain some degree of “fairness for free” without a loss of predictive performance. The AI Now Report is an annual publication that provides a critical perspective on the state of the field, and it highlights problems in real-world deployed systems as well as limitations of the technologies including fair AI methods. Although it’s always valuable to look at the most recent edition, the 2019 AI Now Report is one that has stood the test of time (Crawford et al., 2019).

For an overview of the main issues in AI safety, including the alignment problem, see Hendrycks (2021). Krakanova (2020) explains the problem of specification gaming, and her website maintains an extensive and frequently updated list of examples of it.3 Bostrom (2012) is a classic paper on the dangers of advanced AI and how it might go rogue. In an interview, Meredith Whittaker provides a counterpoint to the current alarmism around possible existential threats from AI and reminds us that there are more pressing issues that we perhaps ought to focus on instead (Chan, 2023).

Part II: More advanced machine learning schemes

We have seen the basic ideas of several machine learning methods and studied in detail how to assess their performance on practical data mining problems. We also addressed data preparation methods and discussed the ethical concerns that arise around these methods and how to mitigate them. Now we are well prepared to look at more powerful and advanced machine learning algorithms. Our aim is to explain these both at a conceptual level and with a fair amount of technical detail so that you can understand them fully and appreciate the key implementation issues that arise. Because of the nature of the material this second part of the book differs from Part I in how you can approach it. Most chapters can be read independently, except that Chapter 9, “Extending instance-based and linear models,” Chapter 10, “Deep learning: fundamentals” and Chapter 11, “Advanced deep learning methods” build on each other incrementally, as do Chapter 13, “Probabilistic methods: fundamentals” and Chapter 14, “Advanced probabilistic methods.”

There are substantial differences between the simple methods described in Chapter 4, “Algorithms: the basic methods,” and the more sophisticated algorithms required to achieve state-of-the-art performance on many real-world problems but the principles are the same. So are the inputs and, in many cases, the outputs—the methods of knowledge representation. But the algorithms are more complex (e.g., they may have to be extended to deal with numeric attributes, missing values, and—most challenging of all—noisy data).

Chapter 4, “Algorithms: the basic methods,” opened with an explanation of how to infer rudimentary rules and went on to examine probabilistic modeling and decision trees. Then we returned to rule induction and continued with association rules, linear models, the nearest-neighbor method of instance-based learning, clustering, and multi-instance learning. In Part II, including the Appendices, we develop all these topics further and also encounter some new ones.

To maximize accuracy in practical applications advantage can often be gained by combining multiple models. A wealth of practical experience has shown that ensembles of models are often necessary to squeeze out the last drops of predictive accuracy. Chapter 8, “Ensemble learning,” introduces various popular methods of ensemble learning—bagging, boosting, and randomization, including the renowned random forest variant—before going on to show how boosting can be interpreted as a form of additive regression, a statistical model-building approach. A major drawback of most ensemble techniques is lack of interpretability but alternating decision trees and related tree-based approaches offer the prospect of high accuracy while also providing insight. Finally, we examine stacking, an intuitive method for combining a diverse set of models to maximize accuracy.

As the name of the chapter implies, Chapter 9, “Extending instance-based and linear models,” extends instance-based learning methods and linear models. There was a resurgence of interest in linear models with the introduction of support vector machines, a blend of linear modeling and instance-based learning. These select a small number of critical boundary instances called “support vectors” from each class and build a linear discriminant function that separates them as widely as possible. This instance-based approach transcends the limitations of linear boundaries by making it practical to include further terms in the function that allow quadratic, cubic, and higher-order decision boundaries. The same techniques can be applied to the perceptron described in Section 4.6 to implement complex decision boundaries and also to least squares regression. An older but also very powerful technique for extending the perceptron is to connect units together into multilayer “neural networks.” We cover all these ideas in Chapter 9, “Extending instance-based and linear models.” These ideas form the basis for deep learning methods, which we describe in depth later in Chapter 10, “Deep learning: fundamentals,” and Chapter 11, “Advanced deep learning methods.” Chapter 9, “Extending instance-based and linear models,” also describes classic instance-based learners, developing the simple nearest-neighbor method introduced in Section 4.7 and showing some more powerful alternatives that perform explicit generalization. The final part of the chapter extends linear regression for numeric prediction to a more sophisticated procedure that comes up with the tree representation introduced in Section 3.3 and goes on to describe locally weighted regression, an instance-based strategy for numeric prediction.

Up to now most of the techniques described in this book have twin goals: maximizing predictive accuracy and producing comprehensible models. Chapter 10, “Deep learning: fundamentals,” however, breaks away and focuses exclusively on maximizing modeling accuracy; it makes no attempt to provide insight by generating interpretable models. Here we enter the domain of “deep learning,” the idea of learning very complex artificial neural networks that implicitly extract increasingly more abstract representations of the underlying patterns in a dataset. We first cover the nuts and bolts of deep feedforward networks, including commonly used loss functions and activation functions, before delving into the details of training and evaluating deep networks, including hyperparameter tuning, data augmentation, and pretraining. Next we introduce a particular type of feedforward network, called a convolutional neural network, that reduces the number of parameters to be learned by weight sharing. We also describe autoencoders, which are network models for unsupervised learning, and recurrent networks, which are designed for sequential data. Chapter 10, “Deep learning: fundamentals,” closes with some pointers to software implementations of deep learning methods.

In Chapter 11, “Advanced deep learning methods,” we consider more recent and advanced topics in the area. First we discuss methods for generating realistic data such as artificial photographic images or artworks, automatically. These generative AI techniques include generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders (VAEs), and diffusion models. We then discuss advances in neural networks for natural language processing (NLP), beginning with word embedding methods for learning representations of dictionary words and building toward the transformer, a neural network architecture based on the concept of attention, which has revolutionized the field of NLP and beyond, with consequences that have already made shockwaves in our daily lives. We close this chapter with several other advanced but practically important topics, including adversarial examples that can be used to deliberately “fool” a deep neural network into making incorrect predictions, knowledge distillation methods for reducing the size of a model while retaining its performance, and deep reinforcement learning methods at the intersection of deep learning and traditional artificial intelligence, which have cracked the nut of creating an AI-based system for playing the game of Go better than the world’s best professional players.

The main focus of this book is on supervised techniques for machine learning, although we also consider unsupervised learning in the form of clustering and association rule mining. However, there are other, less conventional learning settings. In fact, we have already encountered one in Chapter 4, “Algorithms: the basic methods”—multi-instance learning (although it can also be interpreted as a form of supervised learning with bag-based examples). Chapter 12, “Beyond supervised and unsupervised learning,” covers more advanced techniques for multi-instance learning than those in Chapter 4, “Algorithms: the basic methods.” We also look at semisupervised learning, which, by combining supervised and unsupervised learning, promises a tantalizing opportunity to exploit unlabeled data for learning more accurate classification and numeric prediction models.

Chapter 13, “Probabilistic methods: fundamentals,” covers probabilistic modeling approaches that go far beyond the simple Naïve Bayes classifier introduced in Chapter 4, “Algorithms: the basic methods.” We begin with a review of some fundamental concepts, such as maximum likelihood estimation, that form the basis of probabilistic approaches. Then we examine Bayesian networks, a powerful way of extending the Naïve Bayes method to make it less “naïve” by accommodating datasets that have internal dependencies. Next we consider how clustering can be viewed from a probabilistic perspective as fitting a mixture of probability distributions to a dataset. This is essentially a form of density estimation, and we also discuss the alternative approach of kernel density estimation to model the distribution of a dataset.

Except for the brief review of foundations at the beginning, Chapter 13, “Probabilistic methods: fundamentals,” is fairly light on mathematics. Chapter 14, “Advanced probabilistic methods,” addresses material that requires a more mathematical approach. We look at general approaches for fitting models with unknown variables—hidden attributes that are not explicitly included in a dataset—before considering truly Bayesian methods for estimation and prediction. The next big topic is how to represent probability distributions using graphical models such as factor graphs. We will encounter probabilistic principal component analysis and Markov random fields, as well as (probabilistic) latent semantic analysis and latent Dirichlet allocation, two well-known models for working with text data. We will also see how to efficiently compute probabilities for tree-structured graphical models using the sum-product and max-product algorithms.

Chapter 15, “Moving on: Applications and their consequences,” provides an outlook and overview of applications. We discuss learning from massive datasets and data streams, consider the use of domain knowledge, and provide an overview of application areas such as text mining, web mining, computer vision, and speech recognition before briefly discussing the scenario of adversarial learning—learning with a malevolent teacher. We then discuss application areas where there are ethical concerns around the use of these technologies and their impacts on our society as a whole.

The Appendices contain further information on more detailed and technical topics. Appendix A, “Theoretical foundations,” contains the mathematical fundamentals necessary to understand some of the more technical material in the book. Appendix B, “The WEKA workbench,” explains the WEKA data mining software toolkit and how to use it. In Appendix C, “Implementation details of trees and rules,” beginning with decision tree induction, and working up to a full description of the C4.5 system, we cover a landmark decision tree program that is one of the most widely used workhorses of machine learning. Next we describe decision rule induction. Despite the simplicity of the idea inducing rules that perform comparably with state-of-the-art decision trees turns out to be quite difficult in practice. Most high-performance rule inducers find an initial rule set and then refine it using a rather complex optimization stage that discards or adjusts individual rules to make them work better together. We describe the ideas that underlie rule learning in the presence of noise and then go on to cover a scheme that operates by forming partial decision trees, an approach that has been demonstrated to perform well, while avoiding complex heuristics. Following this we take a brief look at how to generate rules with exceptions, which were described in Section 3.4, and examine fast data structures for learning association rules. Appendix D, “Technical details of deep learning,” covers topics that are mathematically dense, including the mathematical derivation of the backpropagation algorithm, calculations of gradients for convolutional neural networks, and stochastic neural networks such as Boltzmann machines, restricted Boltzmann machines, and methods for constructing deep neural network architectures based on them. These topics remain important knowledge for deep learning scholars but are no longer essential for typical deep learning practitioners.

Chapter 8 Ensemble learning

Abstract

A powerful way to improve performance in machine learning is to combine the predictions of multiple models. This involves constructing an ensemble of classifiers—for example, a set of decision trees rather than a single tree. We begin by describing bagging and randomization, which both use a single learning algorithm to generate an ensemble predictor. Bagging perturbs the input data using random resampling; randomization introduces a random component into the learning algorithm. The two can be combined, yielding the so-called “random forest” predictor when applied to decision tree learning, along with a variant called “rotation forests.” Decision tree learners are also commonly used when building an ensemble using the so-called “boosting” algorithm, which generates an ensemble classifier sequentially by iteratively improving on the ensemble built so far. We discuss the seminal AdaBoost.M1 algorithm and then review the closely related additive regression procedure from statistics, which also constructs an ensemble predictor in a sequential error-correcting manner. A key issue with ensemble learners is how to generate an interpretable model from the ensemble of trees. One way is to equip decision trees with option nodes (option trees); another is to add logistic regressions at the leaf nodes (logistic model trees). Bagging, and the other ensemble learners covered heretofore, construct a homogeneous ensemble, generating each ensemble member using the same learning algorithm. An obvious alternative is to generate each ensemble member using different learning algorithms, in which case it is often useful to learn a meta-model to combine the predictions of the various members, a technique called “stacking.”

Keywords

Ensemble learning; bagging; randomization; boosting; additive regression; additive logistic regression; option trees; alternating decision trees; logistic model trees and stacking
