Credit: James Foulds

Each column of the table is a word embedding (a.k.a. a word vector) for the corresponding word, denoted vw for word w. The dimensionality K of the embeddings is a user-selected hyperparameter. Word embeddings use the similarity of vectors to encode similarity of meaning. Here, the highlighted words fox and dog are two words that describe somewhat similar animals, and they have similar vector representations. A very different word, such as jumps, would have a very different embedding (Fig. 11.3).

Also observe that the two occurrences of the word the in the document have the same embedding. This is because word embeddings have a unique word embedding for each word in the dictionary but do not have a unique embedding for each token. In contrast, more recent language models such as BERT can learn contextual embeddings that differ for each token depending on their context.

The semantic relationships between pairs of words can also be captured by the difference between their vectors. In fact, quite surprisingly, analogy relationships can often be identified by vector arithmetic. In many word-embedding models the analogy question, “Man is to woman as King is to ____?” can be solved by calculating

vKing − vman + vwoman,

which results in a vector approximately equal to vQueen (Fig. 11.4).

Word2vec Models

Models and associated learning algorithms have been developed to recover these word embeddings automatically from data. One of the word2vec models produces continuous representations of words by training a neural bag-of-words model to predict words given their context. Because word order in the context window is not captured, this is known as the “Continuous Bag of Words” (CBOW) model. In the CBOW model each word w in the dictionary is associated with a vector-space embedding vw with k dimensions. Given a corpus of training documents, the model learns these embeddings from data by training a classifier that uses them to predict each word token in the corpus based on its context, that is, the words in a small window before and after the current word (Fig. 11.5).

Suppose the size of the context window C is two words. Then the CBOW will try to predict “brown” given its preceding two words (“The,” “quick”) and its following two words (“fox,” “jumps”) and so on for the other words in the document. (Of course, one can also predict the words at the beginning and the end of the document by lopping off words from one side of the context window. In the original 2013 paper by Tomas Mikolov et al., the context window size was C = 4, although they used C = 10 in follow-up work.)

To predict the current word token wi, the CBOW needs to convert the word embeddings in its context, context(wi), into a single feature vector. It achieves this by simply averaging the word embeddings in the context: $v_{\mathit{avg}}\left( w_{i} \right) = \frac{\sum_{j:w_{j} \in \text{context}{(w_{i})}}v_{j}}{\left| {\text{context}\left( w_{i} \right)} \right|}$. Predictions are made using a log-bilinear model, that is, a formulation that is similar to multiclass logistic regression, but both sides of the dot product are learned:

$p\left( \mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}}, \middle| ,{\text{context}\left( \mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}} \right)} \right) = \frac{\exp\left( {\mathit{v}_{\mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}}}^{\intercal}\mathit{v}_{\mathit{avg}}\left( \mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}} \right)} \right)}{\sum_{\mathit{k} = 1}^{\mathit{V}}{\exp\left( {\mathit{v}_{\mathit{k}}^{\intercal}\mathit{v}_{\mathit{avg}}\left( \mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}} \right)} \right)}}.$

We can view this model as a simple neural network with a softmax activation in the output layer. The mapping of vocabulary words to embeddings can also be viewed as a layer in the network, called a projection layer.

The other word2vec model, called the skip-gram, has a slightly different prediction task to train the embeddings. Instead of predicting the word given its context, as in the CBOW, the skip-gram aims to predict the context given the word (Fig. 11.6). These probabilities are once again modeled via a log-bilinear model:

$p\left( \mathit{w}_{j}, \middle| ,\mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}} \right) = \frac{\exp\left( {\mathit{v}\prime_{\mathit{w}_{\mathit{j}}}^{\intercal}\mathit{v}_{\mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}}}} \right)}{\sum_{\mathit{k} \in \text{context}{(\mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}})}}{\exp\left( {\mathit{v}\prime_{\mathit{w}_{\mathit{k}}}^{\intercal}\mathit{v}_{\mathit{w}_{\mathit{i}}}} \right)}}.$

The skip-gram model encapsulates a linguistic theory called the distributional hypothesis. In brief, as famously stated by an early proponent of the theory, J.R. Firth, the theory states, “You shall know a word by the company it keeps.” More concretely, the distributional hypothesis posits that words with similar meanings tend to occur in similar contexts; that is, their probability distributions over neighboring words are similar to each other. Thus, we can potentially use this “distributional similarity” to estimate meaning similarity. The skip-gram very directly implements the distributional hypothesis by way of the word embeddings as intermediaries between distributional similarity and meaning similarity. The word vectors encode the distributions of context words. By design, words that have similar distributions over context words will have similar vectors. And when words have similar vectors, we conclude that they have similar meanings (Fig. 11.3).

Training Word2vec Models

The CBOW model is trained via stochastic gradient descent on the log-likelihood objective function. Here, the normalization constant for the softmax requires computing V terms, the size of the vocabulary, which can be very large, slowing down computation. This computation can be reduced by using the hierarchical softmax approach, which represents the vocabulary as the leaves of a Huffman binary tree, with shorter codes (corresponding to shorter paths through the tree to a leaf node) given to frequent words. In the ideal case where the Huffman tree is perfectly balanced, this would reduce the computational complexity from O(V) to O(log2(V)).

Like the CBOW, the skip-gram is ideally trained by maximizing the log-likelihood objective function; it also has a computational challenge in that normalizing the distributions, necessary to compute the log-likelihood and its gradient, scales linearly in the size of the vocabulary. To address this the hierarchical softmax approach can once again be used. Alternatively negative sampling is a simpler—and consequently more popular—approach. Instead of performing a multiclass classification of the context words wj vs. every other word in the dictionary, negative sampling performs a binary classification of each context word wj vs. a randomly chosen alternative word. In practice, several (e.g., 10) such alternative words (“negative samples”) are drawn, and the model is trained to distinguish between the true context words and the negative samples. Negative sampling is a simplification of a related technique called noise-contrastive estimation (NCE), which follows a similar strategy but which more properly accounts for the noise distribution. Hence, asymptotically approaches the log-likelihood objective function as the number of negative samples approaches infinity but is a bit slower and may not be necessary to achieve the goal of learning word embeddings. It is important to note that the training objectives for CBOW and the skip-gram are merely convenient proxy objectives that enable the recovery of word-embedding representations. Since we only really care about the word embeddings we obtain by the procedure, we are free to approximate the objective function so long as good embeddings are found. The authors of the original word2vec papers (Tomas Mikolov et al. 2013) found that negative sampling was sufficient for this task.

Depending on your target application, training word embeddings from scratch on your own problem-domain-specific dataset using the earlier algorithms may or may not be the best choice. There is often a trade-off between the domain-specific information contained in a domain-specific dataset and the sheer magnitude of generic internet-scale big data corpora that contain a lot of information about language and general knowledge about the world. While a model trained on the domain of interest will generally be best if you have sufficient data, in other cases it can be valuable to leverage big data. Pretrained word embedding models, trained on internet-scale big data, offer the power of big data and the convenience of a model that has already been trained by someone else. In practice, you could choose to either:

  1. 1. Train word embeddings from scratch on your target corpus,
  2. 2. Download pretrained word embeddings trained on generic big data and use them off-the-shelf,
  3. 3. Fine-tune pretrained embeddings on your target corpus, or
  4. 4. Learn embeddings as part of training a more sophisticated deep neural network model, potentially using a pretraining and fine-tuning approach for the embedding component of the model.

The pretraining and fine-tuning approach in options 3 and 4 is often effective since it leverages both generic big data and task-specific small data in a sensible way. The benefits of this approach extend beyond word embeddings to more powerful LLMs.

A key insight of the word2vec research papers was that ingesting enormous amounts of text data is crucial to the performance of language models. At the time that these methods were published (circa 2013), the simplicity of the word2vec models was crucial in scaling them to very big datasets. More recently, with improvements in computational power, particularly due to GPU and tensor processing unit (TPU) resources, and advances in deep learning architectures and algorithms, these models have been superseded by more sophisticated deep neural networks (DNNs). Powerful DNN-based language models still generally make use of word-embedding representations as components of the overall architecture. The word embeddings in a DNN can be initialized randomly or via one of the aforementioned approaches.

Document Classification with Deep Neural Networks

Many NLP tasks can be cast as document classification. The document categorization task is perhaps the most obvious example, in which documents are categorized based on their content or themes, such as whether news articles are about sports or the weather. Sentiment analysis, which aims to predict whether the tone of a piece of text is positive or negative, such as whether a product or movie review expresses a positive opinion, can also viewed as a task that maps documents to class labels. There are many possible document classification tasks. Other examples include language identification, in which we must detect the language that the document is written in; authorship ascription, in which we aim to identify the author of a document (who might be different from person who claims to be the author); and spam classification, in which emails are flagged as unsolicited emails intended for marketing, phishing, fraud, or other undesirable purposes.

A key challenge in document classification is that documents are sequential in nature and thus are not explicitly in a fixed length representation, so standard supervised learning algorithms do not immediately apply. A simple—and often effective—approach to resolve this is to extract fixed-length representations of the documents before applying a standard feed-forward neural network (or, indeed, any other classifier). Classically, this was often done via count-based features, where there is a feature corresponding to each word in the dictionary. Options include binary features (with a one if the word occurs at least once in the document or zero otherwise), bag-of-words features (where the features correspond to the number of occurrences of each word in the document), and term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF × IDF) features. In TF × IDF we account for the fact that in the bag of words representation, commonly occurring words tend to get the highest values even though these words are often the least informative ones. This is done by down- weighting the counts of words that occur in most documents (Section 6.3).

Another simple option is to include features for each word in the document up to a fixed document length of N word tokens while clipping the end of longer documents down to length N and padding shorter documents with dummy values until they reach length N.

The approaches for obtaining fixed-length representations of documents we have discussed so far do not encode the meanings of words relative to each other. To achieve this we can instead use document embeddings (i.e., learned representations of documents). A straightforward approach for obtaining document embeddings is to average the word embeddings for all the word tokens in each document. This is equivalent to adding the word embeddings’ vectors in an end-to-tail fashion, which we could visualize as taking a step in each word embedding’s direction for each word token in the document, then dividing the length of the vector by the number of word tokens. Alternatively, there are models that learn document embeddings directly such as doc2vec. These document embedding models can outperform the simple averaging approach but are more complicated to implement. More recently, transformer-based language models such as BERT, which we will discuss later, have proven effective at learning document representations and currently achieve state-of-the-art performance on most NLP tasks.

Once a fixed-length document representation is obtained, we can apply a feed-forward neural network to predict the class labels. If pretrained document or word embeddings are used in the initial representation, we have the option to either hold those embeddings fixed while training or fine-tuning the classification model or to update the embeddings during training. The latter may perform better but is only feasible if sufficient task-specific data and computational resources are available.

Alternatively, we can instead directly address the sequential nature of text data by applying neural network architectures that handle sequential data. Convolutional neural networks can be applied to the sequence of tokens in a document using one-dimensional convolution, where we slide convolutional filters over the word tokens to identify patterns that occur within the convolutional window (i.e., a window of several words before or after the current token, similar to the context windows used in word2vec). Each filter identifies the presence of one type of pattern in a document, and many such filters are used simultaneously, each producing a corresponding feature, producing a feature vector that can be processed by additional convolutional or dense layers. However, since CNNs only consider a small convolutional window at once they cannot model long-range dependencies, such as between words at the beginning and end of a sentence.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are another option that do not have this problem. While simple RNNs suffer from vanishing gradient issues due to the necessity of backpropagating through the input sequence as well as through the layers, effectively making them behave like much deeper neural networks, more sophisticated RNNs including long short-term memory (LSTMs), bi-directional LSTMs, and gated recurrent unit models keep track of a “long-term memory,” which helps to address vanishing gradients. These models have been successfully used for many deep learning NLP tasks, and this approach was popular for several years in the 2010s. However, at the time of writing, even these sophisticated methods have been mainly supplanted by transformer-based large language models, which process a context window of text in parallel rather than sequentially while still capturing long-range dependencies, unlike CNNs.

Unsupervised and Self-Supervised Training of Large Language Models

Large language models, which learn models of sequences of words based on very large datasets, are the keystone of recent progress in NLP. The size of the training datasets is an enabling factor in the success of these models as it allows them to learn the linguistic patterns present in natural language and to even capture knowledge about the world that is present in text. One crucial challenge in training LLMs is a lack of labeled text data compared to the amount of unlabeled text data that could be obtained from large-scale unannotated text corpora including books, the internet, social media, and so on.

There are several key ideas that enable training LLMs without fully labeled data. The first idea is self-supervised learning—using an auxiliary task, for which labels can be automatically extracted without human annotation, to train the model. For example, the skip-gram word2vec model learns embeddings by predicting the words in the context of a given word. This task was invented for the sole purpose of training a model that obtains good embeddings, and the labels are extracted from the text itself automatically, without requiring human annotation. Self-supervised learning can be considered to be “in between” the unsupervised and supervised learning paradigms as it shares aspects of both.

The second key idea is the encoder-decoder architecture, based on autoencoders (see the previous chapter). Similarly to autoencoders, these models consist of two component networks; an encoder and a decoder. The encoder network maps the input (in our case, input text data) to a latent embedding representation that captures the important semantic information in the input. The decoder network then maps the embedding to the desired output. While autoencoders use the decoder to reproduce the input based on the embedding representation, in the more general encoder-decoder architecture the output could be something else of interest, that is, the next token in the document or the translation of the input text into another language.

To elaborate the latter case, the task of machine translation (MT) is to translate from one language to another (e.g., from English to French). If neural networks are used, this is called neural machine translation (NMT), and when using statistical models it is called statistical machine translation (SMT). NMT methods currently generally outperform SMT approaches and are deployed in the Google Translate service. Seq2Seq is a classic NMT model that uses an encoder-decoder architecture. Its training data pairs corresponding sentences in the two languages. The encoder learns to represent the input sentence with an embedding, and the decoder then converts the resulting embedding to the output language. The final hidden state from the encoder’s recurrent network is the embedding that provides the “context” information for the decoder to use to do the translation. The encoder and decoder are both deep LSTMs. In the original paper, each of these submodels had four LSTM layers. The two modules can also be used alone; some other models use only an encoder (e.g., BERT), and others use only a decoder (e.g., GPT).

A third idea, which is not essential to training LLMs but which proves highly beneficial, is attention—modeling which of the words in the input to pay more attention to or focus on the most. We will discuss this in the next section.

Attention

While the Seq2Seq model’s encoder-decoder approach is intuitive and was an important step forward, a downside of the approach is that a single, fixed-length representation must represent all the information in the entire sentence, and this would be expected to become increasingly difficult as the length of the sentence increases (a fact that is borne out in empirical studies). The RNNsearch model improves over Seq2Seq by allowing its decoder to look back over the input document and decide which words it should pay the most attention to in generating the next token in the translation. This attention mechanism produces weights for each word in the input sentence that sum to one via a softmax neuron. The context vector ci that the decoder uses as its input in predicting the next token in the translation at position i is simply an average of the hidden states (i.e., the embeddings hj at each token j of the input produced by the encoder), weighted by their attention weights αij:

ci = ∑jαijhj.

Here, the attention weight αij is intended to represent the probability that the jth word in the input corresponds to (or is at least informative of) the ith word in the translated output. More generally, attention weights are learned weights that ascribe importance to parts of the input, by analogy to the cognitive process of attention where humans decide to focus on things that are salient while ignoring things that are irrelevant to their current situation (Fig. 11.7). In NLP attention weights are typically applied to the tokens in the input, where tokens can be words, or at the subword level such as for syllables.

11.3 Transformer Architecture

The NMT models we’ve discussed so far use recurrent neural networks such as LSTMs. These models process the data sequentially, which is a major computational bottleneck. In RNN models the sequence must be processed one token at a time, which slows down processing depending on the length of the sequence, and this processing can’t easily be parallelized via a GPU or TPU. Convolutional neural networks are another alternative, and these models can be parallelized. However, CNNs can’t directly model long-range dependences, which are important for many NLP applications, including NMT.

To resolve this situation, researchers from Google proposed the transformer, an architecture that aims to avoid RNNs and convolution by only using attention. This enables more parallelization than RNNs while still capturing long-range dependencies. While their stated goal was to speed up the training of LLMs, the transformer approach also led to dramatic improvements in NLP performance. Though much of this improvement may be due to the larger-scale training that parallelization enables, other benefits of the architecture likely play a role, including the ability of transformer models to consider an entire sentence (or more) at once, and the effectiveness of attention in guiding the focus of the model to salient parts of the text. Its application has extended past NMT to become the state of the art in LLMs and their application to the majority of NLP tasks and beyond into other areas including computer vision. We will now discuss the components of transformer-based language models.

Scaled Dot-Product Attention

As we discussed earlier, attention is a neural network technique for determining which part of some data to focus on. The transformer model uses a specialized version of attention, called scaled dot-product attention. We will view attention using an information retrieval metaphor, where the items of interest that we might attend to (such as the other words in a sentence) are analogous to webpages that we are searching for, and the information that determines what is currently important (e.g., the current word) is analogous to a search query. The items are assumed to have a vector embedding, called a key, which determines its relevance to the “query,” which also has an embedding. An item’s key need not be the same as its value, which is the vector embedding that we will use to represent it going forward, if it does indeed turn out to be salient. Then, attention can be understood as trying to “retrieve” the values of items whose key is relevant to the query by assigning relevance scores (a.k.a. attention weights) according to the similarity between the key and the query.

We will process multiple queries simultaneously. Let Q be a matrix containing nq queries, with each row corresponding to a query’s dk-dimensional query embedding, let K be a matrix containing ni keys with each row corresponding to an item’s dk-dimensional key embedding, and let V be a matrix containing ni values with each row corresponding to an item’s dv-dimensional value embedding. The embeddings in Q, K, and V are all model parameters that can be learned from data or in some cases provided in advance as pretrained embeddings. Scaled dot-product attention is calculated as (Fig. 11.8):

$\text{Attention}\left( {\mathit{Q},\mathit{K},\mathit{V}} \right) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{\mathit{Q}\mathit{K}^{\intercal}}{\sqrt{\mathit{d}_{\mathit{k}}}} \right)\mathit{V}.$

Here, for each query in Q, the softmax produces attention weights over the items. The softmax takes as input the dot products between queries and keys, scaled by a factor $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}$ that aims to prevent the dimensionality of the vectors from having an impact on the scale of the outputs. Applied to all of the queries at once, the softmax produces queries by items matrix A of attention weights, whose rows sum to one. After multiplying this matrix A by V, the final output of scaled dot-product attention is an nq × dv matrix, where each row contains the output for a query, consisting of an average of the items’ value embeddings weighted by their attention weights.

In some cases, we want to exclude some of the items from obtaining any attention. In transformer-based language models, for example, we sometimes want to prevent the model from looking at words that are later in the document so that we are predicting the “future” based only on the “past.” A variant of the method, called masked scaled dot-product attention, replaces the input to the softmax with  − ∞ for any item that should be excluded for a particular query, effectively forcing its attention weight to be zero.

Multihead Attention

As we mentioned before, the goal in transformer-based language models is to replace RNN and CNN architectures with something that addresses their limitations. This means that we need to design the architecture so that it has at least as much representational power as those modules do. Specifically, CNNs use multiple filters to create the representations at each layer, where each filter captures one type of pattern or feature. With multiple filters together in a single CNN layer, each capturing a different pattern, the layer outputs a multidimensional vector representation where each dimension captures different and complementary properties of the data to pass enough relevant information to the subsequent layers. Similarly, RNNs used multiple RNN units per layer to capture multiple patterns, producing a multidimensional representation at each RNN layer of the network.

In transformers we need an analogous approach if we are to replace RNN and CNN layers using only attention. The corresponding concept is called multihead attention. The idea is to perform scaled dot-product attention multiple times, each with its own learned Q, K, and V parameter matrices. Finally, the representation learned from a multihead attention module is the concatenation of the outputs of each of these attention functions.

While the Q, K, and V parameter matrices could in principle be learned separately from scratch for each head, in practice, to reduce the number of parameters to learn, the attention heads share common initial Q, K, and V matrices but the ith head has its own unique projection matrices for each of these parameter sets, WiQ, WiK, and WiV, respectively. Multiplication by these matrices maps the shared parameters to head-specific values while also reducing the number of dimensions of the outputs. A final shared projection matrix WO is used to linearly project the concatenated outputs of all the heads to the target dimensionality for the layer’s representation, dmodel. More formally, the overall multihead attention module, which comprises a layer in a transformer neural network model, can be written as:

MultiHead(Q,K,V;WQ,WK,WV,WO) = Concatenate(head1,head2,…,headh)WO,

where:

headi = Attention(QWiQ,KWiK,VWiV).

In the original transformer paper, the authors used h = 8 of these “heads” per layer (Fig. 11.9). We can also once again use masking on the attention heads, in which case such a module is called masked multihead attention.

Transformer Blocks

Having described the multihead attention module, we are finally ready to explain the transformer architecture. Transformer models are deep neural networks that contain stacks of transformer blocks, each of which itself contains several layers. A transformer block consists of two main sublayers:

  1. 1. A multihead attention layer
  2. 2. A feed-forward layer

The multihead attention layer may optionally use masking as needed. The authors of the original transformer paper use a small one-dimensional feed-forward network that is applied identically to each position of its input, consisting of a ReLU layer followed by a linear layer. The upshot is that in each transformer block, the multihead attention layer is doing most of the work in processing the input, but the feed-forward layer can make a small adjustment to its output. Alternatively, a fully-connected network could be used.

In practice, there are a couple of other layers that are appended to the two main sublayers. These layers are essentially simply employing the various architectural “tricks” that the deep learning community has developed to help ease the training of deep neural networks. More specifically, dropout and layer normalization are performed after each of the sublayers. (Layer normalization is similar to batch normalization but it normalizes the neurons in a layer, instead of normalizing over data points in a minibatch.) Finally, there is a residual connection around each sublayer. See Fig. 11.10 for an overview of a transformer block.

By stacking several of these transformer blocks on top of each other, we obtain a powerful deep neural network model. The original paper used N = 6 transformer blocks in each of the modules of their system, an encoder and a decoder, with the overall system designed for neural machine translation. In a language model the final layer is normally a softmax layer that outputs the predicted probability of the next word in the text sequence.

An astute reader will notice that a transformer block takes three inputs (queries, keys, and values) and produces one output, so it is not completely obvious how these modules can be stacked on each other. There are actually several different ways to use a transformer block, depending on how the input data to the block is assigned to queries, keys, and values, which address this point differently. In self-attention, we apply attention internally within a single input sequence. The context sequence that we wish to attend to (the items with keys and corresponding values) is the same as the set of things we wish to make predictions for (the queries). We therefore often set Q = K = V = x, where the input sequence x is represented as an array of embeddings for each token in the sequence.

For global self-attention, we want to process the entire sequence at once so that every position can attend to every other position in the sequence. On the other hand, if we aim to predict the next word in the sequence we cannot look ahead at future words, as that would be “cheating.” So-called causal self-attention uses masking to prevent the model from attending to the current and subsequent words in the sequence, thus preserving this “auto-regressive property.”

In other cases, the items and the queries may be different sets of entities, a scenario called cross-attention. For example, in NMT an encoder may be used to produce latent representations for the input sequence in the first language, and we may wish to give this as input to the decoder, which aims to predict the translated sequence of tokens in the second language. Then we can set K and V to be the context embeddings produced by the encoder and set Q to be the embeddings for the translated tokens.

Positional Encoding

There is one remaining challenge in using the transformer architecture for language models. RNNs and CNNs are effective for natural language data because they explicitly address the sequential nature of such data. RNNs such as LSTMs process the data in a left-to-right fashion, while CNNs slide convolutional filters over each position in the sequence to find local patterns. However, nothing we have described so far regarding transformer models has made use of the information in the sequential ordering of the tokens, and they would need to do so to be competitive with the models that do this. How can they accomplish this?

The solution turns out to be as simple as injecting some information about the position of each token to its representation. First, in the input layer we initially represent each token with a word embedding, capturing the meaning of the word in vector form just like we saw in word2vec. These input embeddings can either be learned or obtained from a pretrained word embedding model. Next, we add a “positional encoding” (PE) vector to each of the input embeddings that is determined by the word’s index in the sequence, thereby making positional information available to the model.

The positional encodings are the same dimensionality as the input embeddings so that they can be added together. The dimensionality of the embeddings is set to dmodel, the same dimensionality that the multihead attention layers will produce. The authors of the transformer model proposed to use sine and cosine functions for even and odd dimensions, respectively:

PE(pos,2i) = sin (pos/n2i/dmodel)

PE(pos,2i+1) = cos (pos/n2i/dmodel)

where pos is the position in the document, i is the dimension in the positional encoding, and n is a scaling constant that the authors set to 10,000. The result is that each dimension of the positional encoding is a sinusoid, and the wavelengths of the sinusoids follow a geometric progression varying between 2π and 2πn. While other functions, or learned positional embeddings, could be used, the sinusoidal approach works well in practice, and it can extrapolate beyond the length of the sequences seen in the training data. Other authors, such as those of the GPT models, have used learned positional embeddings instead.

11.4 Transformer-Based Language Models

We can now combine all of the components we described to create language models using the transformer architecture.

Decoder-Only Architecture

Suppose we want to build a transformer-based language model to predict sequences of words. Such a model is trained to optimize the log-likelihood of each of the words wi in the text corpus given the previous words in the context window of size k:

L = ∑ilog P(wi,|,wi − 1, wi − 2, …, wi − k).

Each word is represented by an input embedding plus a positional encoding vector. The representations are fed into a stack of N transformer blocks, using masked multihead attention to ensure that at each step of the sequence, only previous tokens are used to predict next tokens. In the final layer, the next word wi is predicted using the last layer’s hidden state vector hN and the input embeddings Ve via softmax(hNVe⊺) (Fig. 11.11). The model we have just described is sometimes called a decoder-only transformer architecture because there is no encoder stage, unlike some of the models we will describe later. It is also an autoregressive model, a term borrowed from time series analysis that means the future (here, later words in the sequence) is predicted based on the past (here, previous words in the sequence).

Generative Pretrained Transformers

The GPT series of models from OpenAI are large transformer-based language models. They are variants of the decoder-only architecture. Since they focus on predicting next tokens given previous ones, they excel at generating new text data. ChatGPT, a chatbot based on GPT, has been fine-tuned via a process called reinforcement learning from human feedback, to follow instructions, or “prompts,” given in natural language form. It can provide startlingly human-like and sophisticated responses. The models can also be fine-tuned to solve other tasks, which was a popular approach with the earlier GPT and GPT-2 models. With more recent GPT models, users are instead encouraged to perform “zero-shot,” one-shot, or “few-shot” learning, whereby models can sometimes solve specialized tasks without fine-tuning by instead providing the task to solve, possibly with a small number of examples, in the prompt itself and relying on the system to interpret the prompt and solve the task based on its knowledge obtained from its large natural language training corpora.

The main modification to the decoder-only architecture in the GPT models is to address supervised learning tasks. The model is first trained as a language model, predicting next tokens given previous ones, which is viewed as a pretraining step. The models are then fine-tuned with additional training to perform supervised NLP prediction tasks including reading comprehension tests, summarization, translation, question answering, and so on.

The original GPT model was fine-tuned for each individual supervised NLP task separately. The larger GPT-2 model, trained on a broader corpus, was able to solve several NLP tasks in a zero-shot learning environment, without fine-tuning for each task, by providing a natural language prompt asking the system to solve the task at hand. This was further improved in the subsequent scaled-up and more powerful GPT-3 model, which had a context size large enough to include several examples of the target task in the prompt, frequently achieving state-of-the-art NLP performance for many tasks with just those few examples (“few-shot learning.”) One of the models from the GPT-4 suite includes image data and provides an API to answer questions about user-provided images. The ability of GPT-4 to solve a variety of AI tasks spanning mathematics, coding, medicine, law, and beyond has led some researchers to declare that it is beginning to reach the early stages of an artificial general intelligence (AGI) system. However, at the time of writing, despite its impressive performance GPT is still vulnerable to producing hallucinations, in which it confidently produces incorrect information. See Chapter 15, “Moving on: applications and their consequences,” for a discussion on concerns and issues regarding GPT and other similar LLMs.

Bidirectional Encoder Representations From Transformers

As we have discussed, GPT processes the text data from left-to right, which makes it very good at generating new text. GPT was also motivated by using a single language model to solve many NLP tasks. However, the left-to-right processing is not optimal for this. BERT is an LLM proposed by researchers from Google that uses a “bi-directional” transformer architecture (i.e., it no longer uses left-to-right processing and it can also examine subsequent tokens). BERT models are state of the art at solving downstream NLP tasks via fine-tuning or extracting embeddings to use as features. Transformer-based methods, largely based on BERT, are currently state of the art across much of the spectrum of NLP tasks, which has rapidly revolutionized the field.

The BERT model uses a version of the transformer architecture in which a stack of transformer blocks is used to produce an embedding of the text that can subsequently be used to perform downstream NLP tasks. Since it produces embeddings and not text sequences, we can think of it as an encoder-only architecture. BERT is intended to be used by pretraining the model on a large unlabeled text corpus and then fine-tuning it to solve a particular NLP task. During pretraining, instead of being trained to predict the next token in a sequence, BERT uses a masked language model (MLM) approach. In MLM, to pretrain the model, we simply hide, or “mask,” a random percentage of tokens from the model and ask it to predict them. BERT also uses a second pretraining task, called next-sentence prediction (NSP). In this task we concatenate two sentences with a separator token between them. In some cases the second sentence is one that appears immediately after the first, and sometimes it is another randomly selected sentence. Then we train the model to predict whether the second sentence is the “next sentence.” Both MLM and NSP are self-supervised learning techniques, in which supervised labels are extracted directly from the text itself, as convenient proxy tasks to train a language model. This approach is thus reminiscent of the skip-gram, in which the prediction of context words was similarly chosen as a convenient and effective self-supervision training objective.

BERT processes a pair of sentences at a time so that it can perform NSP. It appends a special “classification token,” called CLS, before the first sentence, and a “separator” token (SEP) in between the sentences. It also adds “segment embeddings” to each token’s input and positional embeddings to indicate whether the token is in sentence one or sentence two. The embedding for the CLS token is often used as an embedding representation of the sentence to use for downstream tasks. The two-sentence format is also convenient for fine-tuning to solve downstream tasks by using question-answer pairs as sentence one and sentence two in the task-specific fine-tuning dataset. Thus the architecture applies generally to many NLP tasks, with little modification to adapt it to new tasks. See Fig. 11.12 for an illustration of the BERT model.

Transformer-Based Neural Machine Translation

The original paper by Google researchers that proposed the transformer architecture, called “Attention Is All You Need,” used it for NMT. Their approach uses an encoder-decoder architecture reminiscent of the Seq2Seq and RNNSearch models that we discussed earlier, yet it uses transformers. Both the encoder and decoder are stacks of transformer blocks (six blocks each in the original paper). The encoder processes the input text in the original language via its multihead attention mechanisms, identifying and processing the relevant portions of the text. The decoder is used to generate the translation, predicting the next token in the translated sequence based on the input text and the translate sequence so far. The decoder uses masked multihead attention to prevent it from attending to tokens that occur after the current token, ensuring that the predictions are made in a strict left-to-right fashion. The encoder does not need to use masking because we do not need to predict the input sentence, only its translation. The translated tokens are predicted via a final softmax layer like for GPT. See Fig. 11.13 for an illustration.

11.5 Adversarial Examples

With deep neural networks being deployed to make consequential decisions about our lives, both big and small, there are inevitably people who would benefit from interfering with DNNs’ outputs. If a financial transaction is legitimately detected as fraudulent, for example, the fraudster behind it would stand to gain by fooling a DNN fraud detection classification model into predicting that the transaction was legitimate. Spam email classification is a similar scenario. In an extreme case, if a person’s enemies are motivated to commit murder they might accomplish it by tricking the person’s autonomous vehicle into behaving dangerously by causing its sensor systems to predict that a stop sign is only a yield sign, or that a red light is green.

Adversaries can engineer these outcomes by constructing adversarial examples, data points that have been perturbed very slightly, ideally imperceptibly to humans, in such a way that their predicted class labels are changed.

While many classifiers are vulnerable to such attacks, deep learning models are particularly at risk because they learn flexible decision boundaries and can overfit to small imperfections in the training data. It is frequently possible to deliberately construct adversarial examples automatically. The adversary does not need to alter the training data (“data poisoning”) or the learning process, since adversarial examples are constructed at test time and exploit existing flaws in the model’s generalization behavior. It is possible to construct adversarial examples even when the attacker does not have access to the internals of the model, though, of course, that would make the attacker’s job easier. The perturbation needed to change the class label may not be detectable by a human observer. Adversarial attacks can even be achieved in the physical world by attaching a sticker with the perturbation pixels onto a surface to be classified, such as a stop sign.

Given a legitimate sample x with class label y, constructing an adversarial example involves finding the smallest perturbation to modify the class label predicted by neural network f(x) to the desired label y*,

$\mathit{\arg}{\underset{\delta_{x}}{\mathit{\min}}\left\| \delta_{x} \right\|\text{s.t.}}f\left( {x + \delta_{x}} \right) = y^{*}.$

(Another version of the problem simply requires the predicted class label to be different than the original one rather than aiming for a target label.) There is a rich literature on how to construct, detect, and mitigate adversarial examples. Constrained optimization methods to solve this problem are a natural and common approach. Although not optimal, a fast and simple strategy, called the fast gradient sign method, is to take a very small step ϵ in the direction of the sign of the gradient (i.e., up or down) for each pixel:

δx = ϵsign(∇xL(f(x;θ),y)),

where L is the loss function and the sign function applies elementwise and returns  + 1 or  − 1 for each pixel. This approach apparently requires access to the model’s internals. This can often be circumvented. Adversarial example attacks frequently still succeed when applied to a proxy model that is trained on the same data and aims to replicate it or to a model that is trained using the DNN as an “oracle.”

11.6 Knowledge Distillation

The success of deep learning is due in large part to the ability to leverage massive datasets to train large, high-capacity models—big data and big models. But big models have their downsides, too. They are expensive to deploy, with substantial computational cost for each prediction made. This computational burden at deployment time can further impede their use on machines with lower computational power, including mobile phones, internet-of-things (IoT) devices such as those used for smart homes, and edge devices. These models are also difficult to interpret due to their complexity. A solution to all these problems is to construct a smaller model that replicates the behavior of the original, complicated model, hopefully with high fidelity. This is called knowledge distillation (KD). The KD approach has been applied in numerous domains including large language models, machine translation, and speech recognition. It also has been used to transfer knowledge between data modalities from video to text.

To perform knowledge distillation we interpret the original, complicated model as a “teacher model” and use it to train a smaller, simpler “student model.” The key insight to doing this is that the teacher model improves over the hard-assigned class labels in the training set by producing class probabilities for them, thus distinguishing which instances are clear-cut members of a particular class and which are rather ambiguous borderline cases. Instead of training the student model directly on the training data, we train it on the training data but with the teacher model’s class probabilities, called “soft targets,” used in place of the class labels. The student model thus has access to the “knowledge” of the teacher model about the instances’ likely class labels. We can achieve this by minimizing the cross-entropy loss based on the teacher model’s class probabilities. However, if the teacher’s class probabilities are all close to zero or close to one, we will not have gained much by using the teacher’s predictions instead of the original labels. To address this, we can access more nuanced relative class probability information by flattening out the class distribution, via changing the “temperature” T of the distribution. Assuming that the last layer has a softmax activation, we write the class probabilities as:

$p\left( {y_{i}\text{|}x_{i}} \right) = \frac{\exp\left( \frac{z_{c}}{T} \right)}{\sum_{c\prime}{\exp\left( \frac{z_{c}^{\prime}}{T} \right)}}.$

Here zcis the logit of the probability of class c under the model. With temperature T = 1 this is a regular softmax unit, while a larger value of T makes the probabilities less extreme. We train the model using a higher value of T, but we convert back to T = 1 when making our final predictions. See Fig. 11.14 for an illustration.

11.7 Deep Reinforcement Learning

We have focused in this chapter on supervised learning, where a “teacher” has labeled the instances used to train the model. Without a “teacher” to keep the system continually informed, learning becomes much more challenging. Consider, for example, the general AI problem, which is often framed in terms of an intelligent agent (e.g., a robot vacuum cleaner). The agent is in an environment, which it perceives using sensors, makes decisions, and acts in the word through its actuators (e.g., wheels). The agent has a task to perform (e.g., cleaning the room), and it must react to the environment and the results of its actions to achieve it. In reinforcement learning, we suppose that the agent receives a rather limited feedback signal in terms of rewards and punishments, letting it know if it did the task well or not. This reward signal may be given after each action the agent takes, or only at the end of the scenario. The agent aims to act so that it achieves the highest possible cumulative amount of reward and the least amount of punishment (which can be viewed as negative reward).

While using deep learning is only one possible approach to reinforcement learning, the field of “deep reinforcement learning” at the intersection of these two areas has proven successful and continues to be promising for several reasons. DNNs can process complicated data such as input from sensors (e.g., cameras or radar). More importantly, DNNs require a lot of data, and simulated reinforcement learning environments can provide an endless stream of such data, facilitating the training of powerful and accurate models. Although rising to prominence in the 2010s, neural network approaches to reinforcement learning were successful as early as 1995 when such a system, TD-Gammon, was able to excel at the game of backgammon. More recently, the rising tide of deep learning has lifted all boats, including reinforcement learning, for many of the same reasons, including increased computational power and improved deep learning architectures.

Several important success stories of deep reinforcement learning came out of DeepMind, now known as Google DeepMind, a British tech startup company which focused on this technology. DeepMind researchers developed a methodology called “deep Q-learning,” which integrated deep learning into the Q-learning algorithm, a “model-free” reinforcement learning algorithm that avoids learning a “transition model” of the environment. They succeeded in developing deep Q-learning networks (DQNs) that could learn to play many Atari games, from scratch, given only the raw pixel values as input. Their systems used CNNs and were trained by playing the games. They could outperform expert human players and special-purpose ML systems in many of the games.

Although challenging, the Atari games did not require much thinking ahead. Remarkably, the DeepMind researchers were able to use their approach to solve one of the long-standing problems in AI, playing the game of Go at the level of expert human players by combining DQNs with a method for thinking ahead. Go is a board game that has simple rules but is exceedingly difficult to master. There are more than 2 × 10170 legal board positions in Go. In comparison, there are an estimated  ≈ 1080 atoms in the observable universe. Its relatively high branching factor had stymied traditional AI and ML methods. The solution, put forward in DeepMind’s AlphaGo system, was to combine deep reinforcement learning with a search strategy, Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS). To estimate which moves are favorable, MCTS selects randomly generated moves that simulate play until the end of the game.

AlphaGo uses deep reinforcement learning to guide the move choices selected by MCTS. It was trained via self-play. AlphaGo has two neural networks: a policy network, which provides shortlist of promising moves, and a value network, which predicts the winner in a given situation. After AlphaGo defeated European champion Fan Hui in an internal match at DeepMind, in 2016 it defeated all-time great Lee Sedol, 4-1, a milestone moment for AI that was just arguably as important as the success of Deep Blue in defeating Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997. The following year, an improved version of AlphaGo, called AlphaGo Master, defeated Ke Jie, the world’s number-one player at the time, 3-0 in a three-match series.

AlphaGo was initialized using supervised learning based on expert human games and included hand-designed features. DeepMind then developed an improved method, AlphaGo Zero, which avoided both human supervision and hand-designed features and was trained completely from scratch with a blank slate. It was also simplified to use only a single DNN to evaluate the board positions, instead of both policy and value networks. AlphaGo Zero outperformed AlphaGo. It initially learned human-like play including known corner sequences, called joseki, but when trained further, it went on to play in a unique style different from humans. In 2017 DeepMind researchers generalized AlphaGo Zero into a system called AlphaZero, which could beat human expert players on other two-player board games like chess and shogi (“Japanese chess”).

AlphaGo and its sibling models have shown us several insights that may extend beyond these systems, in particular:

  • • Combining deep learning with reinforcement learning and traditional AI techniques like Monte Carlo Tree Search has proved an effective methodology for tackling difficult AI problems.
  • • Hand-tuned features and supervised training were initially helpful but ultimately proved limiting. There was a trend toward using raw features and training from scratch.
  • • Simpler models/methods were ultimately better.
  • • There was a trend toward generalizing the methods to multiple tasks. The best methods could solve multiple Atari games or play multiple board games.

11.8 Further Reading and Bibliographic Notes

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are due to Goodfellow et al. (2014), although similar ideas were proposed much earlier by Schmidhuber (1991). Another generative AI approach, variational autoencoders (VAEs), was proposed by Kingma and Welling (2013). More recently, diffusion models, due to Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015), have become popular for generating AI art. Rombach et al. (2022) proposed to apply diffusion models in the latent space of autoencoders, reducing model complexity while generating high-resolution images and enabling a straightforward approach to guide the generation with a natural language prompt.

Natural language processing via neural networks has a long history. The work of Collobert et al. (2011), which argued that deep learning—where features are learned automatically from data—could replace manual feature engineering, was a milestone in showing the promise of deep learning for NLP. The word2vec models, proposed by Mikolov et al. (2013), also represented a turning point, both due to their prominent use of vector-space embeddings for words that are ubiquitous even in today’s sophisticated deep neural network models and due to accelerating the push toward large pretrained language models that ingest as much data as possible. Le and Mikolov (2014) extended this approach to learning document vectors, which are important for many document-level classification tasks. Sutskever et al. (2014)’s Seq2Seq model is emblematic of the pretransformer era of deep learning for NLP, using LSTMs and an encoder-decoder architecture, in this case for neural machine translation. Convolutional networks were also popular for NLP around this time, cf. Kim (2014). Bahdanau (2016) improved over Seq2Seq using an attention mechanism, which paved the way for transformer models, proposed by Vaswani et al. (2017). Transformer-based language models revolutionized the field of NLP, quickly becoming state of the art at most NLP tasks. The GPT series of models from OpenAI, beginning with Radford et al. (2018), proved effective generative models of text, while BERT, due to Devlin et al. (2019), and its successors, proved to be powerful representation learning tools with excellent performance at downstream NLP tasks.

Adversarial examples were first identified by Szegedy et al. (2014), who also proposed the first method for constructing them, via box-constrained limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (L-BFGS) optimization. Goodfellow et al. (2015) demonstrated that adversarial examples are not due to the nonlinearity of deep neural networks; rather, even linear models can suffer from this issue in high dimensions. They used this insight to propose a simple and fast linear approach to generating adversarial examples—the fast gradient sign method—that has proved effective and highly influential. Papernot et al. (2016) formalized the threat model for adversarial examples and proposed more targeted methods for generating them, which exploit knowledge of the DNN architecture to perturb only a small number of features (e.g., pixels) to evade detection while potentially flipping the label to a chosen alternate label. Kurakin et al. (2018) showed that adversarial examples can be exploited in the physical world, when they are perceived via a camera, with important and worrisome implications for physical systems such as IoT devices and autonomous vehicles. Carlini and Wagner (2017) returned to optimization-based approaches, developing more effective methods that can defeat robustness measures designed to protect against these attacks, such as defensive distillation.

Knowledge distillation was first invented by Bucilă et al. (2006) but popularized much later by Hinton et al. (2015), who proposed using temperature-adjusted versions of the teacher model’s predictions as “soft targets” for the student model. Deep Q-networks (DQNs) for deep reinforcement learning were proposed by Mnih et al. (2015), who used them successfully to develop human-level agents for playing Atari games. Silver et al. (2016) combined DQNs with Monte-Carlo tree search to develop AlphaGo, which at that stage had already defeated European Go champion Fan Hui. Silver et al. (2017a) developed AlphaGo Zero, the “tabula rasa” version of AlphaGo that learned completely from scratch, followed by AlphaZero (Silver et al., 2017b), which generalized AlphaGo to achieve superhuman performance in other games like Chess and Shogi.

    7. G. Design a baseline method to compare your method against, which is not a deep neural network.

    Bonus question: Extend your model to account for the user’s relative stances (e.g., if two users in a thread express disagreement with each other, they are likely to be on opposite sides of the issue).

Chapter 12 Beyond supervised and unsupervised learning

Abstract

In many practical applications, labeled data is rare or costly to obtain. “Semisupervised” learning exploits unlabeled data to improve the performance of supervised learning. We first discuss how to combine clustering with classification; more specifically, how mixture model clustering using expectation maximization can be combined with Naïve Bayes to blend information from both labeled and unlabeled data. Next, we discuss how a generative approach for learning from unlabeled data, such as the one based on fitting a mixture model, can be combined with discriminative learning from labeled data. Following that, we consider the “cotraining” method for semisupervised learning, which can be applied when two different views are available for the same data. These two views normally correspond to two distinct sets of attributes for the same instances. Finally, we see how cotraining can be combined with expectation maximization in the so called “co-EM” method to yield further improvements in predictive performance in some scenarios. In addition to semisupervised learning, this chapter also discusses sophisticated techniques for multiinstance learning, which improve on the simple methods presented in Chapter 4, “Algorithms: the basic methods.”

Keywords

Semisupervised learning; combining clustering and classification; expectation maximization; combining generative and discriminative modeling; cotraining; co-EMmulti-instance learning
